clue.text: Most like a penniless pie-fancier

parts.note: the nursery-rhyme boy who met a pieman going to the fair wanted a pie but had no penny; the clue asks for the superlative of his name's adjective

explanation.surface: Someone who loves pies but has no money is being described.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme, Simple Simon asks the pieman for a pie and is told to show his penny first, but he has none. The answer is the superlative of the adjective in his name.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme's hero is called Simple, so whoever most resembles him is the most artless.

clue.text: Seated in proper style

indicators.note: putting the letters of seated into a proper, orderly arrangement signals that they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sits down with decorum and good posture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in proper style' rearranges SEATED, and the whole clue also describes how a staid person sits.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedate person is calm and decorous, which is exactly how someone sits when seated with propriety.

clue.text: Certainly not the light of reason

definitions.text: Certainly not the light of reason

parts.words: Certainly not the light of reason
parts.note: the word means both the glow of the night sky's satellite and foolish talk, which is anything but rational illumination

explanation.surface: Something is plainly not a beacon of rational thought.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is the literal light from the moon; the other is nonsense, the very opposite of reason's light.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonsense or fanciful talk is the opposite of reasoned thinking, and the word also names lunar light.

clue.text: Colossal, this deficit in fuel

indicators.note: this word says the answer is what sits inside the fuel within Colossal, so the fuel's letters around it are taken away

parts.note: coal is a fuel

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on an enormous shortfall in fuel supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in fuel' looks like part of the shortage, but it marks the split: the clue's first word is the fuel wrapped round the deficit, so 'in' strips the fuel away.
explanation.definitionFit: A deficit is a shortfall, an amount lost or missing.

clue.text: To drink with some soldiers is topping

parts.note: to sup is to drink, taking liquid in sips
REME, the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: Having a drink with a few soldiers is declared excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a corps of the British Army. 'topping' is old British slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are old-fashioned praise meaning first-rate or best of all.

clue.text: Treated with sisterly care

parts.note: in British hospitals a senior nurse is called Sister, so care from a sister is the work of a ward nurse

explanation.surface: Someone was looked after tenderly by a female sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: A senior hospital nurse in Britain is called Sister, so 'sisterly care' points to nursing rather than family.
explanation.definitionFit: Tending a patient in hospital is the work done by a Sister on the ward.

clue.text: Topsyturvy state of affairs for rail commuters to Town?

explanation.surface: Commuters heading into London find everything in disarray.
explanation.walkthrough: On British railways the 'up' line runs towards London ('Town') and the 'down' line away, so a commuter to Town uses the up side; the second reading is UP SIDE and DOWN.
explanation.definitionFit: Topsy-turvy means inverted or in disorder; the railway sense splits the phrase into the up side of the line for London-bound trains.

clue.text: A spin round the country

indicators.note: the word spin goes round the letter a, signalling that one piece encloses the other

explanation.surface: Someone takes a quick trip around a nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts SPIN around A, giving S-P-A-I-N.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain is a nation of south-west Europe.

clue.text: An arresting Shakespearian character

parts.note: a constable who arrests the villains in Much Ado About Nothing; arresting means both striking and making arrests

explanation.surface: A striking figure from one of the Bard's plays is wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arresting' seems to mean striking, but it means making arrests: the bumbling constable of Much Ado About Nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogberry is the comic constable in Much Ado About Nothing whose watchmen arrest the plotters.

clue.text: Tenements for women only — on principle ?

definitions.note: the definition is singular while the answer is plural; on principle, these are beliefs held

indicators.note: a place for women only admits no males, so the males are taken out of the word before

explanation.surface: Blocks of flats reserved for women on a matter of principle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for women only' removes MEN from TENEMENTS, leaving the answer. The plural answer against 'principle' is loose: the clue sits on 'on principle'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenets are doctrines or beliefs held as true, the same as principles.

clue.text: Way out swingers

explanation.surface: Some very unconventional people with liberal habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way out' looks like slang for unconventional and 'swingers' like party people, but these are exits and things that swing on hinges.
explanation.definitionFit: Exits from a room are ways out, and hinged panels swing open and shut.

clue.text: It was more interested in the- Fleet than in Fleet Street

definitions.text: It was more interested in the- Fleet than in Fleet Street

parts.words: It was more interested in the- Fleet than in Fleet Street
parts.note: Fleet Street was the home of the British newspaper industry, while the Fleet is the Royal Navy; the group forced men into naval service, not journalism

explanation.surface: A body cared more for the navy than for newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleet Street was London's newspaper district, so 'press' suggests journalists; but these were men who seized recruits for the Royal Navy's fleet.
explanation.definitionFit: A gang that impressed men into naval service worked for the fleet despite its name echoing the newspaper press.

clue.text: It's lost or won by a head

definitions.text: It's lost or won by a head

parts.words: It's lost or won by a head
parts.note: sounds like a horse race decided by a narrow margin, but refers to calling heads or tails on a coin

explanation.surface: Something narrowly decided, like a race won by a head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by a head' suggests a close horse race; it means the head side of a flipped coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Flipping a coin is won or lost when it lands heads or tails.

clue.text: In this day Americans have cause to celebrate

definitions.text: In this day Americans have cause to celebrate

parts.words: In this day Americans have cause to celebrate
parts.note: the American holiday on the Fourth of July marks freedom from British rule; the answer is the word that, put after In and before day, names it

explanation.surface: A remark that nowadays Americans have reasons to rejoice.
explanation.walkthrough: Put the answer between 'In' and 'day' and you get the name of the American national holiday on the Fourth of July.
explanation.definitionFit: Placed after 'In' and before 'day', the word completes the name of the US national holiday.

clue.text: Unpleasant sphere of medical activity

parts.note: sounds like a disagreeable field of medicine, but a sphere is a round object, here a tablet taken as a remedy

explanation.surface: A disagreeable branch of medical work is described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sphere' seems to mean field of work; it is a small round tablet. A bitter pill is also something unpleasant one must accept.
explanation.definitionFit: A bitter pill is literally an unpleasant-tasting tablet and figuratively a hard thing to accept.

clue.text: What's fine about it? Being conclusive

indicators.note: the word fine sits about, or around, the word it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks what is good about a thing, being decisive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's' is only a link; 'about' is a container signal, not 'concerning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something finite has bounds and an end, so it comes to a conclusion.

clue.text: He could, but doesn't, make ladders

definitions.text: He could, but doesn't, make ladders

indicators.note: making something out of the letters of ladders means rearranging them into a new word

explanation.surface: A craftsman is capable of making ladders but chooses not to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make' rearranges LADDERS. The letters could make him, and a leatherworker could make ladders but works on harnesses instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A saddler is a craftsman who makes saddles and harness, not ladders.

clue.text: In a' word, a rum colour

definitions.text: In a' word, a rum colour

parts.words: In a' word, a rum colour
parts.note: a flower name joined to a colour to make one compound word, describing a pure, spotless shade that is an odd pairing

explanation.surface: Someone sums up, briefly, an odd hue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rum' means odd here, not the spirit: a flower and a colour are joined into one hyphenated word meaning spotless.
explanation.definitionFit: Lily-white is a compound naming the pure whiteness of the flower, used for anything spotless.

clue.text: Reverses for established defenders

parts.note: set means fixed or established
backs are defending players in football or rugby

explanation.surface: Defeats suffered by long-standing defensive players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reverses' is a noun, misfortunes, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Setbacks are reverses of fortune, checks to progress.

clue.text: No 'doubt he has something to put up with

definitions.text: No 'doubt he has something to put up with

parts.words: No 'doubt he has something to put up with
parts.note: sounds like someone with a burden to endure, but the person puts things up, building them, and so has equipment for raising things

explanation.surface: A man surely has some trouble he must tolerate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up with' seems to mean tolerate; it means raise, as one who erects scaffolding or buildings carries tools for raising them.
explanation.definitionFit: An erector is a person who erects or builds structures, putting them up.

clue.text: It lends colour to travel of course

parts.note: red is a colour
a car is a means of travel

explanation.surface: Something brightens up a journey, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: REDCAR is a racecourse in north-east England. 'of course' looks like 'naturally' but points to the racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Redcar is a seaside town in north-east England with a well-known horse-racing course.

clue.text: "And quoted odes, and — five-words long." (Tennyson)

parts.note: a line from Tennyson's The Princess, completed by the precious stones that are short quotations sparkling on time's forefinger

explanation.surface: A gap-fill from a line of Tennyson's poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in The Princess reads 'jewels five-words-long / That on the stretch'd forefinger of all Time / Sparkle for ever'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson calls brief memorable phrases precious gems, filling the gap in his line.

clue.text: Door-man starts early in the year

definitions.text: Door-man starts early in the year

parts.words: Door-man starts early in the year
parts.note: a doorkeeper whose title comes from Janus, the Roman god of doorways, who also gives his name to the first month

explanation.surface: A doorman begins work in the opening weeks of the year.
explanation.walkthrough: The word begins with JAN, short for January; both come from Janus, Roman god of doors and beginnings.
explanation.definitionFit: A janitor is a caretaker or doorkeeper, from the Latin for door.

clue.text: Scintillatingly gay gallants

parts.note: lively young dandies are an old meaning of the word, and scintillating suggests the tiny flashes thrown off by a fire

explanation.surface: Dashing young men full of brilliant cheer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gay' has its old sense of merry; a spark was a lively, showy young man, and sparks also scintillate.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparks were fashionable young gallants, and scintillations are glinting flashes.

clue.text: Like Cassius's Colossus in the finest part of Yorkshire?

parts.note: best means finest
Yorkshire was divided into three ridings, North, East and West

explanation.surface: A Shakespearian giant is located in the best area of Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: In Julius Caesar, Cassius says Caesar 'doth bestride the narrow world like a Colossus'. Yorkshire, an English county, was historically split into three administrative Ridings.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassius pictures Caesar standing astride the world like the giant statue, legs spread over it.

clue.text: Little Alexander appears to have plenty of grit

definitions.text: appears to have plenty of grit

explanation.surface: A young boy named Alexander seems to be very brave.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandy is a Scottish pet form of Alexander; 'grit' looks like courage but means sand.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandy is a familiar short form of Alexander, and sandy ground is full of gritty particles.

clue.text: Give the captives back in exchange

indicators.note: giving the captives back means writing that word for them backwards

parts.note: POWs are prisoners of war

explanation.surface: Hand over the prisoners in a prisoner exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns POWS, prisoners of war, round. SWOP is an older spelling of swap.
explanation.definitionFit: To swop is to trade one thing for another, an older spelling of swap.

clue.text: Heroic poetry 'of the silver screen ?

explanation.surface: Stirring verse from the cinema.
explanation.walkthrough: An epic is a long heroic poem, and also a lavish spectacular film.
explanation.definitionFit: Long narrative verse about heroes is the original sense; a sweeping blockbuster movie is the cinema sense.

clue.text: Fond antic of a bosom friend

annotationWithheld.why: Fond antic of a bosom friend: the answer is an anagram of FOND ANTIC, but no word signals the anagram except 'antic' itself, which is also fodder, so one word does two jobs.
annotationWithheld.clue: Fond antic of a bosom friend

clue.text: Conventual poet?

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a member of a convent writes verse.
explanation.walkthrough: A prior heads a priory, a religious house; Matthew Prior was an English poet of around 1700.
explanation.definitionFit: A prior is a monastic superior, a member of a religious house, and Matthew Prior was an English poet.

clue.text: The whirlpool's opposite number

parts.note: in Greek myth the whirlpool Charybdis faced a six-headed monster across the strait, so the monster is its counterpart

explanation.surface: Someone asks what faces the whirlpool across the way.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Odyssey, Charybdis is a whirlpool facing the rock monster across the Strait of Messina; 'between Scylla and Charybdis' means between two dangers.
explanation.definitionFit: Scylla was the sea monster on the rock opposite the whirlpool Charybdis.

clue.text: Game little insects

parts.note: sounds like plucky small bugs, but the bat-and-ball game shares its name with the chirping insects

explanation.surface: Some brave small bugs are described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like plucky; it names the sport cricket, which is also the chirping insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Crickets are chirping insects, and cricket is also a bat-and-ball sport.
